query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an active‐learning driven sampling protocol into ab initio free-energy calculations will substantially reduce the number of high-cost molecular dynamics evaluations needed to accurately capture all relevant entropy contributions (vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration couplings) across solid and liquid phases near the melting point, without significantly sacrificing fidelity compared to full ab initio MD.
generation.material_initial_state: Elemental, binary, and multicomponent high-entropy alloy systems in both solid and liquid states near their melting points.
generation.intervention: Implement an active-learning framework that adaptively identifies and selects the most informative atomic configurations along the free-energy integration paths. In these selected points, full ab initio evaluations are performed, while unsampled regions are estimated through a trained surrogate model.
generation.conditions: Applied under high-temperature conditions near fusion (melting) for materials ranging from elemental and binary systems to complex multicomponent high-entropy alloys (HEAs); the technique is primarily targeted for the integration paths that contribute to vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron-vibration coupling.
generation.structural_mediator: The free-energy integration path across the solid-liquid transition, which inherently controls the accurate capture of entropy contributions and phase free energies.
generation.mechanism: The active-learning protocol minimizes redundant high-fidelity DFT evaluations by identifying key configurations where changes in local energetic and vibrational environments are most pronounced. This selective sampling maintains accurate tracking of free energy differences while significantly reducing computational effort relative to exhaustive MD sampling.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction (potentially 2–5× speedup) in computational cost while achieving phase free energy estimates within an error margin of approximately 10 meV/atom compared to explicit ab initio MD and TOR-TILD, thereby accurately reproducing key observables such as melting temperature.
generation.baseline: Full explicit ab initio MD evaluations as well as the TOR-TILD method, which, while effective for elemental and binary systems, become prohibitively expensive for complex high-entropy alloys.
generation.boundary: The method is expected to be effective for systems with up to five or more principal elements and under conditions near the fusion temperature. Its performance outside high-temperature regimes or in systems with extreme compositional complexities remains untested.
generation.uncertainty: The precise speedup and accuracy retention may vary with the complexity of the material system. Uncertainties include the selection efficiency of the active-learning algorithm in extremely multicomponent environments and its ability to capture all subtle entropy contributions.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform free-energy evaluations on a series of materials including an elemental metal, a binary alloy, and a representative high-entropy alloy near their melting temperatures using both the active-learning enhanced method and full ab initio MD. Compare the obtained phase free energy differences, vibrational entropy contributions, and melting temperatures.
measurements: Total computational time and number of high-fidelity DFT evaluations
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the active-learning approach produces free energy differences that deviate by more than ~10 meV/atom compared to full ab initio MD, or if the computational cost reduction is less than a factor of 2, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields. To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations. The simulation results are validated by a comparison to first-principles Korringa-Kohn-Rostoker (KKR) - Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) [KKR-CPA] calculations for the HEA structural properties (lattice constants and bulk moduli), relative stability, pair probabilities, and high-temperature short-range ordering. The simulation (MD)-derived properties are in quantitative agreement with KKR-CPA calculations (first-principles) and experiments. We study Al x CrCoFeNi for Al ranging from 0 ≤ x ≤2 mole fractions, and find that the HEA shows large chemical clustering over a wide temperature range for x < 0.5. Polymorphism, which describes the occurrence of different lattice structures in a crystalline material, is a critical phenomenon in materials science and condensed matter physics. Recently, configuration disorder was compositionally engineered into single lattices, leading to the discovery of high-entropy alloys and high-entropy oxides. For these novel entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter with extremely high structural stability, is polymorphism still possible? Here by employing in situ high-pressure synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction, we reveal a polymorphic transition from face-centred-cubic ( fcc ) structure to hexagonal-close-packing ( hcp ) structure in the prototype CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy. The transition is irreversible, and our in situ high-temperature synchrotron radiation X-ray diffraction experiments at different pressures of the retained hcp high-entropy alloy reveal that the fcc phase is a stable polymorph at high temperatures, while the hcp structure is more thermodynamically favourable at lower temperatures. As pressure is increased, the critical temperature for the hcp -to- fcc transformation also rises.

The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. decision.trend: Early studies in fusion property evaluation transitioned from empirical‐potential methods that mainly targeted phase‐transition temperatures to explicit ab initio molecular dynamics approaches that capture full free‐energy differences—including vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions—in both solid and liquid phases. TOR-TILD represented a further refinement by increasing throughput for elemental and binary systems; however, as system complexity increases toward multicomponent high-entropy alloys, the same exhaustive sampling becomes prohibitively expensive due to the vast configurational space.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved challenge is to obtain high-fidelity fusion free energies (with all entropy contributions retained) for multicomponent systems at a computational cost that is markedly lower than that of both explicit ab initio dynamics and TOR-TILD. In other words, how to reduce the sampling burden in complex systems without sacrificing the necessary accuracy in free-energy differences across phases.
decision.why: Building on the trend of incorporating advanced sampling strategies into free-energy evaluations, the next methodological hypothesis is to use an active-learning framework that selectively identifies the most informative configurations needed along the solid and liquid free-energy integration paths near melting. This lever minimizes redundant high-cost DFT evaluations while ensuring that all crucial entropy contributions are maintained. It naturally follows the cue that explicit ab initio methods, while accurate, are too expensive for high-entropy systems, and that TOR-TILD’s acceleration diminishes when faced with multicomponent complexity. A decisive test would be to benchmark phase free energies and derived observables (e.g., melting temperature) in elemental, binary, and high-entropy systems against full ab initio MD results with an error margin below a set threshold (for example, ~10 meV/atom), thereby falsifying or validating the hypothesis.
